title: 2026GdP1 – Turtle graphics, loops and functions
overview: In this digital worksheet you first draw a square with a turtle and then entire rows of squares. You will learn to group repeated commands into loops, define your own functions and change their behaviour using parameters. The goal is to **turn every task green**: check both your drawing and the requirements for your code, and answer the reflection question. You can work with Snap blocks, Python or the function-based Java editor.
turtleIntroduction: A **turtle** is a virtual drawing pen. While the pen is down, every movement draws a line. `forward(100)` moves the turtle forwards by 100 steps. **Turn right** rotates it clockwise: in Python, `right(90)` turns through 90 degrees. The turtle starts facing right. With right turns, a square therefore hangs below the line on which the turtle starts. The palette shows the available blocks; use the corresponding commands in the Python editor. Open the editor, recreate the target figure and check your solution with the tests. In Java, use `Turtle.forward(100)` and `Turtle.right(90)`. In Snap, start your program with “when green flag clicked” and attach your drawing commands below it.
loopIntroduction: **Loops** save repeated code. A “repeat n times” block runs its contents n times. In Python you can use `for i in range(n):` with an indented block of commands. Now draw the same square using a loop. The count n is a nonnegative whole number, for example 4. In Java, you can use `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... }`.
nestedLoopsIntroduction: Let us make the figure a little more complex: a loop can contain another loop. This lets you describe both the sides of a square and a whole row of squares. **Pen up** (`penup()`) lets you move without drawing; **pen down** (`pendown()`) resumes drawing. In Java the pen commands are `Turtle.penUp()` and `Turtle.penDown()`.
functionIntroduction: **Functions** group related commands under a name. You define them once and can then call them repeatedly. In Snap, use “Make a block” to create a block named `quadrat`. In Python, start with `def quadrat():` and indent the function body. Keep the function name `quadrat` in both languages so the tests can find it. In the Java editor, create a method named `quadrat`, for example `static void quadrat()`. You edit methods directly; the editor keeps them in its structured class model.
parameterIntroduction: Functions can receive data: **parameters** make their behaviour adaptable. In Java, such functions are also called methods. This worksheet supports Snap, Python and Java. A suitable Java method signature is `static void quadrat(double distanz)`. Create a block `quadrat` with an input named `distanz`, or a Python function headed `def quadrat(distanz):`. Pass the desired side length when calling it. Keep these names unchanged for the tests. Here, the gap always means the empty distance from one square edge to the next.
alternationIntroduction: Let us try a more complex example: the side lengths should now alternate. Think about combining a loop with suitable parameter values.
orientationIntroduction: One more challenge: both the size and orientation change. A second parameter might help. The sequence is **down, down, up, down, down**: as before, the squares hang below the shared line; only the third lies above it. Hint: a left turn is the same as `right(-90)`.
task1Instruction: Recreate the target figure: a square with side length **100**. Use only **forward** and **turn right**. Write every drawing command separately; use neither loops nor your own functions.
task2Title: Task 2 · A square with a loop
task2Instruction: Draw the same square with side length **100** again. This time use a **loop**, but do not define your own function yet.
task3Instruction: Recreate **five squares in a row**. Every square has side length **100**, and each gap between neighbouring square edges is **100** steps. Use loops, but **no functions of your own**. Do not draw connecting lines between squares.
task4Instruction: Recreate the same row of **five squares** with side length **100** and gaps of **100**. Use loops and define your own function or block named **quadrat**. Call this function to draw the squares.
reflectionInstruction: In your own words, describe **two different advantages** of structuring code using loops and your own functions. More than two meaningful advantages are welcome.
reflectionScaffolding: Offer one short guiding question without giving away the answer: What would need to change in a program if a different figure were required? Would several places need editing? Alternatively, ask how the learner would explain the program to someone else and which recognizable subtasks could guide that explanation. Give just one small prompt at a time.
reflectionGrading: Assess the reflection answer. CORRECT requires at least two distinct, relevant advantages of structuring programs with loops and functions; more are allowed. Examples include changes in one central place instead of many edits, shorter code with less duplication, fewer errors, improved readability and recognizable subtasks, reuse, and meaningful function names that make explanations easier. The list is not exhaustive: accept other justified benefits and answers in German or English. Two restatements of the same advantage count only once. One relevant advantage is PARTIALL_CORRECT; no relevant advantage is INCORRECT. Do not require code or particular technical terms.
task5Instruction: Draw five squares in a row with side lengths **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500**. Each gap between neighbouring square edges remains **100**. Use loops and a function **quadrat** with a parameter named **distanz**. Do not draw connecting lines.
task6Instruction: Draw five squares with side lengths **100, 200, 100, 200 and 100**. As before, all hang below the shared line, and each gap is **100**. Use loops and the function **quadrat** with parameter **distanz**.
task7Instruction: Draw five squares with side lengths **100, 200, 100, 200 and 100**, with gaps of **100**. Their orientation is **down, down, up, down, down**: the third square lies above the shared line and the others hang below it. Use loops and the function **quadrat** with parameter **distanz**. Add a second parameter for orientation if helpful.
testOnlyCommands: Uses only forward and right turns
